executive_summary: CHF/JPY closed at 191.117 on 30 October 2026. That is 191.117 yen per franc, and a rising pair means a stronger franc. The pair is up 0.47% over one month, down 1.99% over three months, down 4.94% over six months and down 1.44% over a year. It sits at the 19th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 188.035-204.143. The main bilateral story is a contest between two safe havens. The Bank of Japan is tightening from 1.25% while the SNB holds at 0%, so the franc is replacing the yen as the funding currency of choice. Against that, Japan's energy bill, its fiscal turn and Europe's sovereign stress all favour the franc. Each standalone currency view is Neutral tactically, but the cross brings out what each one had netted away against the dollar. Three things stand out: an energy gap that makes the pair behave like a long position in LNG prices, the widest sovereign-quality gap in G10, and speculators who are short francs and long yen at the same time, both at 25-week extremes. The tactical stance is Neutral, conviction 2 (score +0.052). The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 2 (score -0.109), with a six-month base case of 186.50 and selling on rallies into 192.20-192.50 as the preferred entry. The caveat is that the strategic score clears the Bearish threshold by only 0.009, and a hawkish SNB forecast on 10 December could push it back to Neutral.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On long-run measures the franc is extremely expensive against the yen. The BIS real effective rate is 98.37 for the franc against 66.61 for the yen (September 2026). World Bank PPP factors put fair value for CHF/JPY near 104.30, which leaves spot about 83% above parity, or a 45% yen discount. The franc's real rate is at its lowest in 33 months while the yen's sits near the 21st percentile of the same window, so the gap is very large but has stopped widening. The current level embeds a yen discounted for negative real rates, a five-month goods deficit and fiscal expansion, and a franc priced for its surplus and haven status. Neither PPP gap has a record of closing on a 1-6 month horizon. Valuation matters here as an asymmetry, not a timing signal: any energy relief for Japan acts on a deeply cheap yen. Spot sits at the 19th percentile of the closing range (21st on an intraday basis), 308 pips above the 11 September closing low and 1,303 pips (6.38%) below the closing high.

market_context.recent_regime: From May to July the pair held a 199-204 range while carry funded in yen worked. The joint US-Japan intervention of 30-31 July broke it, taking the pair from 200.89 to 193.97 in three sessions. An August recovery to 198.74 failed, and a second leg on 2-11 September took it to 188.03 as BoJ pricing firmed ahead of the September hike. Since then, two forces have locked the pair into a 187.60-192.50 band: the October European sovereign shock, which revived the franc's haven bid, and Japan's energy and fiscal headlines on one side, against the widening rate gap and franc-funded carry on the other. One analysis frames this as a tradable asymmetry: the geopolitical premium has favoured the franc because Japan depends heavily on energy imports, while BoJ hawkishness and intervention risk support the yen.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Annualised policy carry is -125bp for a long CHF/JPY position (SNB 0.00% minus BoJ 1.25%, both as of 27 October 2026); a short collects it. Separately, the funding premium implied by the December 2026 / March 2027 CME franc and yen futures, crossed and observed 29 October, is 147.5bp a year; under covered interest parity this is the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve, and it is not the policy differential. Carry-to-vol is -0.17 on policy carry and -0.20 on the futures premium against a 7.308% three-month implied vol estimate; because the vol estimate runs low, the true ratio is probably smaller in magnitude. Inside the cross the yen is the higher yielder by 125bp, though against the rest of G10 both are funders, and the gap is widening in the yen's favour as the BoJ hikes and the SNB holds. Carry is modest relative to vol, so it does not set direction alone. It does make the strategic short carry-positive, which is unusual for a funding cross. Forward points apply the 147.5bp premium flat across tenors.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy differential works against the franc. The SNB policy rate is 0% and the Bank of Japan's call rate is 1.25%, both as of 27 October, so the base currency yields 125bp less than the quote. The front end has moved the yen's way. The Swiss 2-year yield fell from 0.263% at end-September to 0.18% on 30 October as December SNB hike pricing faded to about 6bp. Over the same period the 2-year JGB held near 1.90% on the back of roughly 75% December BoJ pricing, which leaves the 2-year gap near 172bp. At the long end, the Swiss 10-year at 0.47% sits about 230bp below the 10-year JGB at 2.77% on 30 October closes. The monthly OECD series for September shows a 246bp gap, but that reading is a month old and not a live level. Neither bank decides inside the four-week window: the SNB's next assessment is 10 December and the BoJ meets on 18 December. Over the next four weeks the channel is therefore carry plus communication. Governor Ueda speaks on 6 November and the BoJ has said it will keep raising rates, while the SNB has given no rate bias. Carry favours the yen and the trend favours it a little more, but both are largely priced in, which keeps confidence in the mid-50s.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential is more likely to widen against the franc than to narrow. Our base path has the BoJ at 1.50% after 18 December, with a second hike in play at the 22 January meeting (which carries the Outlook Report) or by April. The Bank's 30 October statement said it will continue to raise the policy rate, Takata dissented in favour of an immediate move, and swaps price close to 75bp of BoJ tightening over twelve months. The SNB, by contrast, has a conditional forecast that keeps inflation inside 0-2% at a 0% rate, and its 10 December quarterly assessment is expected to hold. The franc's only route to a narrower gap is a 2027 SNB hike. Bloomberg Economics puts that no earlier than March 2027, and we give it about 30%, which places it beyond the scheduled decisions in front of us. On that path the gap moves from 125bp to 150-175bp. The BoJ leg is mostly priced, so the unpriced risk runs both ways: a BoJ pause would be the main pair-positive surprise, and a hawkish SNB forecast on 10 December the main offset on the franc side. The transmission is direct. CHF/JPY links the two lowest-yielding G10 currencies, so the relative rate path, not the level of global yields, decides which one funds carry trades, and Rabobank has noted the franc becoming an alternative funding currency as the BoJ tightens.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is the clearest in this pair. Swiss headline CPI was 1.0% in September with core at 0.5%. Japanese CPI was 2.1%, with the ex-fresh-food measure at 2.1% and the ex-fresh-food-and-energy measure at 2.4%. Japan is therefore running above its target while Switzerland sits in the lower half of its 0-2% band. Real policy rates are strikingly close, about -1.0% in Switzerland and about -0.85% in Japan, so the data move the pair through the relative policy response rather than the real-rate level. Growth runs the other way. Swiss Q2 GDP rose 1.5% q/q on a pharmaceutical surge, while Japan grew 0.3% q/q in Q2 and the JCER consensus for Q3 is barely positive at +0.08% annualised. Inside four weeks the releases are evenly balanced. Swiss October CPI on 3 November could revive SNB pricing if it prints 1.2% or higher. A negative Japanese Q3 GDP print on 16 November would strengthen the BoJ's cautious wing. National CPI on 20 November could lock in December if core reaches 2.4%. Japanese data carry more weight for the pair because the BoJ is the bank that is moving, but with the releases pointing both ways the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the inflation gap argues for more BoJ tightening than SNB tightening. The BoJ's 30 October Outlook Report kept FY2026 core CPI at 2.5% and raised FY2027 to 2.6%. Firms expect prices to rise 2.5-2.6% a year in the Tankan, and a 5.01% Shunto supports a wage-price cycle. The SNB's conditional forecast, by contrast, averages 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in 2027, the board sees hardly any second-round effects, and Swiss wage growth is subdued. Swiss inflation is rising from a low base and could reach 1.2-1.4% on oil. That is the franc's one route to a 2027 hike, but it stays inside the SNB's band and does not force action. Japan's food consumption-tax cut from April 2027 will mechanically take about a point off measured CPI. That is a communication risk at the edge of the horizon, and the BoJ has said it will look through it. Growth favours Switzerland, but the pharma-driven Swiss figures are volatile and the KOF barometer and PMI have both turned lower, so growth is unlikely to move the SNB before the BoJ moves again. On balance the macro data give the BoJ more reason to keep going, a mildly pair-negative signal held at low confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: In a pair of two safe havens, the sign of the risk factor depends on where the stress comes from rather than how much of it there is. The live stress is European and sovereign. The OAT-Bund spread reached 152.5bp on 20 October, the widest since 2011, alongside a global bond sell-off driven by debt levels in which Japan's public debt above 200% of GDP features. Both channels favour the franc, which regained its haven role in October on the strength of Swiss fiscal stability. The energy channel favours the franc too. Brent near USD 110-123 and JKM LNG at USD 32.84/MMBtu hurt Japan's terms of trade far more than Switzerland's, and during the escalation phase of the Gulf war this year the yen weakened rather than rallied. The yen's advantage is global deleveraging. An AI-led equity sell-off, already visible in an 8.2% one-month fall in the Nikkei, would force carry unwinds in which the yen, as the larger funding stock, tends to outperform. Over four weeks the more likely stress events (French political failure, a post-midterm escalation with Iran, a weak JGB auction) favour the franc. A broad deleveraging is less likely with VIX at 17.2 and US investment-grade spreads at 89bp. The factor is mildly Bullish for the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the contest between the two havens has no stable winner. A resolution of French stress or a Gulf ceasefire would remove the two channels that currently favour the franc. A Gulf settlement would also help the yen more, through lower energy costs, while an escalation would do the opposite. A broad equity de-rating from record US levels would favour the yen in two ways: repatriation by Japanese investors, whose net foreign assets were about USD 3.6tn at end-2024, and unwinds in yen-funded crosses. The franc, however, now competes as a funding currency, and its own speculative short would also be covered in such a move. Gold, the cross-asset signal most associated with the franc, fell about 7% in October from a peak above USD 5,500, which removes a supportive signal. Each plausible scenario favours a different leg and we cannot rank them, so the factor is Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Positioning on the two legs adds up rather than cancelling. In the CFTC data for the week to 27 October, leveraged funds were net short 17,502 franc contracts, their largest short in the 25 reports since May. Asset managers were net long 91,191 yen contracts, also a window extreme, and the legacy speculative yen long jumped to 101,600 contracts, beyond the 80,000 level that has marked stretched yen longs in past cycles. Being short francs and long yen at the same time amounts to a crowded short CHF/JPY exposure across speculative accounts. The franc short sits with fast money, which covers first in a stress event, and the yen long was built in a month with no BoJ decision. Both are vulnerable to the same kinds of news. A softer BoJ message or a negative Japanese GDP print would hit the yen long, and a hot Swiss CPI print or French escalation would hit the franc short. Options on the two dollar pairs lean the same way, with franc calls and yen puts both bid against the dollar. Contrarian pressure is therefore pair-positive over four weeks, which is why this factor is Bullish even though the fundamental factors around it lean towards the yen.

The SNB, by contrast, has dropped its increased willingness to intervene and bought only CHF 1.4bn of foreign currency in Q2. We expect the speculative extremes to normalise early in the horizon, after which structural flows dominate. Those flows lean mildly to the yen through repatriation and to the franc through the Swiss surplus, so the factor is Neutral.

tactical.historical_analogue: No clean positioning-driven reversal specific to this pair is documented. tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is positioned for the yen to keep outperforming as the BoJ tightens and the SNB holds. That view is already in the positions: the yen long was added while the rate outlook barely changed, and the franc short sits with the accounts quickest to cover. Without a BoJ decision until 18 December, any wobble in Japanese data, or any European stress that triggers franc buying, would force both legs to cut at once.

Positioning then becomes a mild headwind for the pair rather than support, which is why we stay Neutral rather than contrarian-bullish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two external balances diverge sharply. Switzerland's current account surplus was CHF 23.7bn in Q2, about 9.2% of GDP. Japan's surplus of about 5% of GDP is almost entirely investment income that is reinvested abroad. Its goods trade has been in deficit for five months: September's JPY536.6bn deficit was nearly three times the forecast, and crude imports rose 51.1%. Terms of trade are the channel. JKM LNG at USD 32.84/MMBtu, up 27% in a month and nearly 200% over a year, and Brent near USD 110-123 raise Japan's import bill far faster than Switzerland's, where energy is about 3.5% of the CPI basket. Direct trade between the two is small and roughly balanced: Switzerland exported USD 9.3bn of goods to Japan in 2024 and imported USD 7.7bn, a USD 1.6bn Swiss surplus. Bilateral flows therefore do not move the pair; the effect runs through each economy's global balance. Japan's October trade release on 17 November should show the full LNG spike, and we expect a deficit of JPY0.8-1.2tn against JPY0.54tn in September. The factor is Bullish for the pair over four weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the energy gap between the two economies is the dominant external force. Winter LNG demand coincides with JKM projected near USD 34 at end-quarter, which keeps Japan's goods balance in deficit. Switzerland's surplus, meanwhile, is supported by a real exchange rate at its lowest in 33 months. The IMF projects a Swiss surplus of 6.2% of GDP for 2026, and the settled 15% US tariff rate on Swiss goods and pharmaceuticals removes the main export shock. Valuation is the counterweight, and it is large. The BIS real effective rate is 98.37 for the franc against 66.61 for the yen. World Bank PPP puts spot roughly 83% above parity, which is the same as a 45% yen discount. Our standalone research on both currencies treats these gaps as structural rather than tradeable within six months. Even so, the yen's extreme cheapness raises the payoff from any energy relief. A Gulf settlement, which we put at 15%, would cut Japan's goods deficit by roughly half and is the main risk to this stance. Bilateral goods trade is too small to matter. The factor stays Bullish for the pair, at lower confidence than the external data alone would justify because of the valuation gap.

LNG/JKM up: negligible for the franc, strongly negative for the yen. Net effect: the pair rises. Gold up: mild franc positive, neutral for the yen. Net effect: the pair rises slightly. Gold's roughly 7% fall in October is therefore a small offset. Taken together, the pair behaves like a long position in energy prices, with JKM the strongest driver and gold a minor one.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two banks' guidance differs in content as well as direction. The BoJ's 30 October statement upgraded its judgement to underlying inflation 'at a level generally consistent with' 2%, repeated that it will continue to raise the policy rate, and drew a hawkish dissent from Takata. Ueda added that the Bank must be vigilant to the risk of inflation overshooting. The SNB's latest message, the 22 October summary of deliberations, carried no rate bias and kept the conditional forecast inside the band at 0%. It did drop the 'increased willingness to intervene', which removes a cap on franc strength, mainly against the euro. Inside four weeks only one side speaks: Ueda on 6 November, followed by the BoJ's Summary of Opinions in the second week of November, while the SNB is silent until 10 December. Japan's Ministry of Finance, having bought about JPY27.1tn of yen this year, is a second credible authority leaning against yen weakness. No Swiss authority leans against franc weakness. Both the timing of communication and its content lean towards the yen, so the factor is mildly Bearish for the pair.

The SNB's 10 December quarterly assessment comes first, the BoJ follows on 18 December, and the BoJ's 22 January meeting carries the Outlook Report. The yen side therefore has the last word in each round of guidance and two chances to deliver. The BoJ's credibility as a normaliser is established after hikes in December 2025, June 2026 and September 2026. Its voting has shifted from two dovish dissents in September to a hawkish dissent in October. Our franc research expects the December forecast to edge 2027 inflation up to 0.9-1.0%, and that is the main risk to this stance. A hawkish forecast is not a hike, though, and the SNB has said nothing that points to a move before 2027. With one bank explicitly guiding to further tightening and the other guiding to an extended hold, guidance favours the yen at moderate confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal gap is the widest of any G10 pair. Swiss general government gross debt is about 38% of GDP, the federal budget ran a surplus in 2025, and every major agency rates Switzerland AAA. Japan's gross debt exceeds 230% of GDP on Fitch's figure, its ratings sit at A+ (S&P) and A (Fitch), and FY2026 debt service exceeds JPY31tn. Japan's fiscal stance is also loosening: the food consumption tax falls from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027, and the Prime Minister has not ruled out extra JGB issuance. The bond market has shown it will charge for this. The 10-year JGB hit 3.135% on 7 October, the highest since 1996, before easing to 2.77%, and in this cycle higher JGB yields driven by supply have weakened the yen rather than supported it. The 5 November 10-year auction is the one test inside four weeks. In October, a global bond sell-off framed around debt levels sent investors into the franc on the strength of Swiss fiscal stability. The factor is Bullish for the pair.

At the same time the BoJ keeps tapering its JGB purchases, so the market must absorb more duration just as issuance rises. That combination risks a higher term premium and a weaker currency together. Switzerland faces only modest structural federal deficits, below 0.5% of GDP, under a constitutional debt brake. Japan has real mitigants: domestic holders own most JGBs, Fitch expects deficits to stay manageable, and global managers have been buying JGBs near 3%. The gap is still large and moving the wrong way for the yen, so the factor is Bullish for the pair at moderate confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For a cross between the two lowest-yielding G10 currencies, dollar liquidity matters through two channels: which leg is the preferred funder of dollar carry trades, and how Japanese and Swiss institutions hedge their dollar assets. Dollar funding is calm. SOFR is 3.94%, inside the 3.75-4.00% range; central-bank swap-line use is USD 170m; and reserve balances are near USD 2.96tn, so neither leg is under funding stress. On the listed futures rolls the franc trades at a 454.8bp annualised premium to the dollar against a 387.5bp policy gap, and the yen at 287.9bp against 262.5bp. The excess is larger for the franc, about 67bp against about 25bp, which makes hedging dollar assets relatively costlier from francs. A December Fed hike on 9 December would keep the dollar on the right side of the smile, where both low-yielders come under similar pressure. Japanese investors' incentive to repatriate, with hedged Treasuries yielding less than JGBs, offsets the franc's role as the cheaper funder. The factor is Neutral.

tactical.score_interpretation: At +0.052 the score is inside the +/-0.10 Neutral band. Breadth, not depth, keeps it positive: five small franc-favouring factors (risk appetite, positioning, external balance, event risk, fiscal) add +0.218, against one heavy yen-favouring factor, relative rates (-0.130), plus guidance (-0.036). This is a stalemate with a slight franc lean, not a directional signal. Scores between -0.10 and +0.10 map to Neutral. Conviction 2 rather than 1 reflects measurable, well-defined offsetting forces. Carry within the cross is modest: about -0.17 on policy rates and about -0.20 on the futures premium, against an estimated 7.31% three-month implied vol. Conviction 2 holds while the score stays between -0.10 and +0.10, December BoJ pricing sits at 65-85% and the OAT-Bund spread at 140-170bp.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Policy & Rates makes the largest single contribution at -0.130. The franc yields 125bp less than the yen, and the gap is set to widen to 150bp if the BoJ hikes on 18 December, although neither bank decides inside the four-week window. Against it, breadth does the work: risk appetite (+0.069), positioning (+0.067), external balance (+0.034), event risk (+0.026) and fiscal quality (+0.022) all favour the franc, while guidance subtracts 0.036. The net score of +0.052 sits inside the Neutral band. Our standalone franc and yen views are both Neutral tactically, so they neither reinforce nor conflict. The cross view pulls out the forces each of them had netted against the dollar. The yen's energy bill and fiscal turn, and the franc's haven and fiscal premium, lean towards the franc, while the one force both rank highest, relative rates, leans towards the yen. Three factors specific to this pair shape the result: the energy gap between the two economies, the widest fiscal gap in G10, and positioning in which speculators are simultaneously at extremes short francs and long yen. Markets price a December BoJ hike at roughly 75% and almost nothing for the SNB, and the listed futures roll charges a franc holder about 147.5bp a year. Any edge lies in the crowded short-franc, long-yen positioning and in stress coming from Europe, both of which are less fully priced than the rate path. The path of least resistance is sideways, with yen-side data deciding the direction. The key dates are Swiss CPI on 3 November, the 10-year JGB auction on 5 November, Ueda on 6 November, Japan's Q3 GDP on 16 November, the trade balance on 17 November and national CPI on 20 November. Conviction is 2: the offsetting forces are well defined and measurable, but the score does not clear the band and its largest component points the other way. A hawkish BoJ Summary of Opinions or Japanese core CPI of 2.4% or more would strengthen the rate factor and pull the score towards zero or below. A Swiss CPI print of 1.2% or more, together with further French stress, would push it towards the Bullish threshold.

Among franc crosses, CHF/JPY is a weaker franc long than EUR/CHF shorts, where the European-stress channel acts directly.

strategic.score_interpretation: At -0.109 the score clears the Bearish threshold by 0.009. Depth on the yen side, from rates (-0.139), guidance (-0.065) and inflation dynamics (-0.051), totals -0.255. That outweighs the franc's external balance (+0.088) and fiscal quality (+0.058), which total +0.146. The other five factors are Neutral. This is a low-conviction Bearish reading that a single change in the SNB's 10 December forecast could move back into Neutral. A score of -0.10 or below maps to Bearish; at a 0.009 margin, with the heaviest franc-side factors structural, conviction is 2. Conviction 2 holds while the score is between -0.10 and -0.20, the BoJ is priced near 2.00% in twelve months and the SNB is priced on hold into mid-2027.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the score is -0.109, just beyond the Bearish threshold, and the stance follows from it. Policy & Rates (-0.139), guidance (-0.065) and inflation dynamics (-0.051) favour the yen. The BoJ has two decisions in the horizon, 18 December and 22 January with the Outlook Report, and guides explicitly to further hikes. The SNB is expected to hold at 0% at its 10 December quarterly assessment, with inflation inside its band. External balance (+0.088 at a 0.16 weight) and fiscal quality (+0.058 at a raised 0.10 weight) favour the franc, on Japan's winter energy bill and widening deficits. Here the standalone views pull in opposite directions: our yen research ranks the yen 2nd of 11 strategically and our franc research ranks the franc 4th, each mildly bullish on its own currency. The pair result is what remains after the yen's stronger policy story is set against the franc's stronger balance-sheet story. Between two low-yielders the policy gap is the bilateral channel that matters most, because the relative rate path decides which currency funds carry trades. Rabobank has already flagged the franc as the alternative funder as the BoJ tightens. Much is priced: the futures roll already discounts 147.5bp a year of franc depreciation against the yen, and swaps carry the BoJ towards 2.00% over twelve months. The edge is therefore narrow and lies mainly in the SNB staying at zero longer than a hawkish reading implies. The path of least resistance is a gradual yen advantage concentrated around 18 December and 22 January. RBC's published path for the pair points the same way, though it predates October's European stress and Japan's fiscal turn. Conviction is 2 for three reasons: the score clears the band by only 0.009; valuation weighs heavily against the franc while energy and fiscal weigh against the yen; and one hawkish SNB forecast on 10 December would erase the margin. A BoJ hold on 18 December, or a Swiss forecast showing 2027 inflation at 1.0% or more, would take the score back into Neutral.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the yen ranks 2nd of 11 in our G10 work and the franc 4th, so CHF/JPY is a middling strategic yen long. It is the only yen long against a G10 peer that earns positive carry, which makes it the cleanest way to own the BoJ normalisation theme without paying the carry seen in USD/JPY or AUD/JPY. But the franc's surplus and fiscal strength make it a tougher opponent than the deficit currencies, so the expected move is smaller than in yen crosses against GBP, NZD or EUR.

November is spent inside the 187.60-192.50 triangle, with the upper edge sold, as Japanese data set December pricing. The 10 December SNB assessment is the first test. A hold with an unchanged 0.8% forecast for 2027 lets the BoJ hike on 18 December take the pair through 189.50 to retest 187.60, with year-end liquidity making the break gappy. The FY2027 Japanese budget in late December may cause a pause or a pullback towards 190.00-191.60 (the round number and the 50-day), which should be sold. The 22 January Outlook Report meeting is the second step, and a break of 187.60 has no computed support until 179.48, so the 186.50 base case can be reached within days of a hawkish January. February-March fiscal year-end repatriation extends the move. Realised vol should run at 5-8%, with spikes around the two BoJ meetings. consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast_source: RBC Capital Markets (Currency Report Card, around mid-August 2026); BofA published 190 target noted for reference
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral (score +0.052): offsetting forces, with relative rates favouring the yen and energy, fiscal, haven and positioning factors favouring the franc over the next four weeks.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish (score -0.109, conviction 2): the BoJ's tightening path and guidance outweigh the franc's external and fiscal advantages over one to six months.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: In line with RBC on direction strategically, since both favour the yen. Tactically we are Neutral, where RBC's path implies modest yen gains through year-end.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: At end-December our path is about 189.00 against RBC's 187, so we are about 200 pips (1.1%) less yen-bullish into year-end. At end-April 2027 our 186.50 is about 50 pips below RBC's 187.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: We share RBC's premise that BoJ tightening drives the yen into 2027, but we weight two bilateral factors more heavily over the next four weeks. First, speculators are at 25-week extremes short francs and long yen at the same time, which leaves the pair exposed to a squeeze. Second, the live sources of stress (French sovereign risk, a debt-led global bond sell-off and Gulf energy) favour the franc over the yen. RBC's forecast also predates three developments: the SNB's 22 October retreat from its increased willingness to intervene, the October fiscal turn in Japan with the food tax cut and possible extra issuance, and the 27% October jump in LNG prices. All three narrow the yen's advantage, which is why our strategic call is only marginally Bearish.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the BoJ delivers in December or January while the SNB holds, the yen leg gains both on spot and on carry, and a holder of yen against francs collects about 147.5bp a year while waiting.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the SNB signals a 2027 hike on 10 December, or the BoJ pauses after weak Q3 GDP, the crowded yen-long and franc-short positioning could unwind sharply against the strategic view, while energy and fiscal factors continue to favour the franc.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge because the factors that favour the franc (risk appetite, positioning, event risk) carry more weight over four weeks and fade over six months. Strategic weights move towards external balance and guidance, and the BoJ's two scheduled decisions arrive inside the strategic window but not the tactical one. Relative rates are Bearish on both horizons; what changes is that over six months the BoJ actually gets to act on its guidance.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: 10-22 December and 22 January: the SNB's 10 December quarterly assessment, the BoJ on 18 December and the BoJ's 22 January Outlook Report meeting. Earlier signals would be Japan's Q3 GDP on 16 November and national CPI on 20 November, which set December BoJ pricing.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Through November, treat the pair as directionless with a squeeze risk to the upside rather than leaning into the strategic yen view. The strategic view becomes actionable once Japan's November data confirm December BoJ pricing, and the SNB's 10 December forecast is the first test it has to survive. Tactically no outright position at spot; the only entry consistent with both horizons is to sell the upper triangle edge 192.20-192.50 at half the strategic size, stop on a daily close above 193.70, target 190.20. Strategic entries: A (50%) sell 192.20-192.50 with a stop on a daily close above 195.00; B (50%) sell a retest of 190.00-190.50 after a 18 December BoJ hike with a stop above 192.80; targets 187.60, 186.50, 182.00. Risk 0.5% of capital per strategic entry; cut Entry A by half before 10 December if Swiss November CPI prints 1.2% or more.

catalysts.rationale: September CPI was 1.0% with core at 0.5%. A print of 1.2% or more would revive December and early-2027 SNB hike pricing from about 6bp and lift the pair. A print of 0.8% or less would confirm the franc's role as a zero-rate funder and support the yen's carry advantage. It falls on a Japanese holiday, in thin liquidity.

This is the one test of Japan's fiscal premium inside the tactical window, after the 10-year fell from 3.135% to 2.77%. A weak auction tail would revive supply fears that have weakened rather than supported the yen in this cycle, lifting the pair. A strong result would confirm the October bond rally.

Ueda's first remarks after the 30 October Outlook Report can move December BoJ odds by 10-15 points either way. A hawkish tone confirms the widening policy gap against the franc, while hedging on December would hit the stretched yen long and push the pair up.

catalysts.event: BoJ Summary of Opinions (30 October meeting; second week of November, exact date approximate)
catalysts.rationale: The anonymous opinions will show how many members besides Takata favour a near-term hike. Several would lift December pricing above 85% and widen the expected policy gap against a silent SNB. It is the most likely tactical trigger for a test of 189.50.

The JCER consensus is only +0.08% annualised, and a negative print, which our yen research puts at 40%, would revive the Board's cautious wing and cut December hike odds. That is the most likely trigger for the crowded yen long to unwind against the franc.

October includes the 27% monthly jump in JKM LNG and the start of winter buying, and a deficit of JPY0.8-1.2tn is expected against JPY0.54tn in September. It makes the energy gap concrete: Switzerland runs a goods surplus while Japan's deficit deepens.

Tokyo's 2.6% ex-fresh-food print points to national core of 2.3-2.5%, up from 2.1%. A print of 2.4% or more would lock in a December hike and the widening of the policy gap to 150bp against a franc on hold, the main tactical risk to the Neutral score.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A hike to 4.00-4.25% pressures both low-yielding legs against the dollar in similar ways, so the direct effect on the cross is small. The projections matter more: an end to hiking would push the dollar towards the bottom of the smile, where both havens gain and Japanese repatriation incentives strengthen.

catalysts.event: Swiss National Bank quarterly monetary policy assessment
catalysts.rationale: A hold at 0% is expected and would leave the franc as the lower-yielding leg ahead of the BoJ eight days later. A conditional forecast showing 2027 inflation at 1.0% or more, or any signal of a 2027 hike, is the main pair-positive risk to the strategic Bearish view and could flip it to Neutral.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting
catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 1.50%, about 75% priced, would widen the gap to the SNB to 150bp and confirm the yen's lead in the haven contest. A hold would be the largest pair-positive event in the horizon, given crowded yen-long positioning and a franc short held by fast money.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 draft budget (due by year-end; week 4 of December, exact date approximate)
catalysts.rationale: The first budget to quantify the food tax cut, cash payments and any additional issuance. A 10-year JGB back above 3.0% on supply would widen the fiscal contrast with Switzerland and, as in October, weaken rather than support the yen. That would cause a pause or a pullback in the strategic decline.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: This is the only scheduled decision in the window that comes with a projection round. Keeping core CPI above 2% through FY2027 and signalling the next hike would extend the yen's rate advantage towards 175bp, while the SNB has no decision until March.

assumptions: Price series: daily closing prices (with open, high and low), 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 191.117 at the 30 October 2026 close. The valuation date of 1 November 2026 is a Sunday, so the two-day gap covers a weekend and no trading session is missing. Every level, distance, pip figure and percentage in this report is measured against that spot.

Data quality: the full history behind the averages and zones runs to 4,920 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30, with 1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars. The 130 sessions shown match the 1-6 month strategic horizon. Weekend-dated rows are excluded throughout, so a 200-day average is a genuine 200-trading-day average.

Moving averages and trend: simple averages of trading-day closes (50, 100 and 200 days, and 200 weeks), computed over the full history. The 200-week slope is +0.2516 yen a week, and the latest weekly close is above it. The data do not give how long the pair has continuously held above it, so no duration is stated.

Support and resistance: zones are clusters of weekly and monthly swing closes, each with a touch count. Distances are to the zone midpoint, with near-edge distances given where relevant. Zones are ranked by touch count. Chart patterns (the symmetrical triangle) and wave counts come from published dealer commentary, not from the computed zones.

Volatility: realised vol is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 1.057 yen (106 pips). Implied vol is an estimate from listed franc and yen options and a realised correlation of 0.486, observed 29 October; it runs low by a median 14.4% against direct quotes and is treated as a floor. No CHF/JPY option is listed on any venue, so no implied-vol percentile, cross risk reversal or barrier data exist; skews are inferred from the two dollar legs.

Carry and forwards: the 147.5bp figure is the annualised spread between December 2026 and March 2027 franc and yen futures, crossed and observed 29 October (45.7- and 136.6-day tenors). It combines the interest differential and the cross-currency basis. Forward outrights apply it flat across 1, 3 and 6 months. The annualised_carry_bps field uses the -125bp policy differential, signed for a long CHF/JPY position.

Rates: policy rates (SNB 0.00%, BoJ 1.25%) are as of 27 October 2026. The 10-year yields in the official monthly series (Swiss 0.59%, JGB 3.05%, gap -246bp) are September readings and are not quoted as live levels. Live comparisons use 30 October daily closes (Swiss 0.47%, JGB 2.77%) and the 29 October JGB 2-year fixing.

Positioning: CFTC data are for the week to 27 October 2026. Percentiles cover the 25 weekly reports since 12 May 2026 (the schema percentile fields are set to 0 for the most-short CHF position and 100 for the most-long JPY position in that window), and the +80,000 yen-long threshold is a long-run rule of thumb.

Trade: bilateral goods trade is IMF Direction of Trade data for 2024. Swiss-reported exports to Japan (USD 9.3bn) and Japan-reported imports from Switzerland (USD 8.2bn) differ, as mirror statistics usually do.

Weights: six weights were adjusted within +/-0.05 per factor and sum to 1.00 on both horizons. Net stances follow mechanically from the weighted score: +0.10 or above is Bullish, -0.10 or below is Bearish, and anything between is Neutral.

Consensus: bank consensus rests on a single bank (RBC Capital Markets, around mid-August 2026). BofA's published 190 target is noted as a reference that has been reached. Model-driven and sentiment-blended forecast pages are not treated as bank research.
Probabilities: scenario probabilities are fixed at 50/25/25. Probabilities for policy decisions, tail events and invalidators are our own estimates unless described as market pricing.

Formatting: dossier dates are set to the valuation date as none was stated in the report; catalyst dates for the BoJ Summary of Opinions (second week of November) and the Japan FY2027 draft budget (late December) are approximated to a calendar date.
